The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services is reminding families who received 2026 Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits to use any remaining funds by Nov. 16.

The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. Under federal requirements, any unused benefits will be returned to the funding source after the expiration date.

Families are encouraged to check their card balances and use their remaining benefits before Nov. 16. However, those who received their child’s card later and were given a different expiration date should follow the date provided.

Families who have not picked up their child’s Summer EBT card or need a replacement may visit the Bureau of Economic Security office on the second floor of the RanCare Building in Tamuning from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.Monday through Friday.

For assistance, families may contact the Summer EBT Call Center at (671)735-7325 or (671)735-7310, or email kidssebtguam@dphss.guam.gov .

Public Health administers the Summer EBT Program locally in partnership with the Guam Department of Education.

item.title: Hybrid Land Use Commission approves school in Tumon, extension for Tamuning subdivision
item.description: The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning. The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning.

The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.

Architect Michael Blas Makio, managing principal at Taniguchi Ruth Makio Architects, said the project would be good for Tumon and good for education.

“Even driving here, we started the really sad exercise of counting the vacant buildings that we're seeing around the island, and that's a really scary growing number, right? So we’ve got to find these viable uses that we can bring into the space,” Makio said.

The vacant mall is located next to Garden Villa Hotel and across from Crowne Plaza Resort.

The Commission also granted a one-year extension for the construction of Oka Villas subdivision, located near Oka Pay-Less and Rosie’s Apartments in Tamuning.

The land has been cleared and utilities are being installed.

The subdivision will have 36 single-family residential lots, a playground and a percolation basin.

item.title: Medicaid program serves more than half of CNMI population, annual report shows
item.description: The Commonwealth Medicaid Agency reported significant gains in healthcare coverage, federal funding and operational modernization during fiscal year 2026, highlighting its role as one of the CNMI's largest healthcare safety-net programs. According to the CMA’s report, the agency served 23,690 active Medicaid beneficiaries during the reporting period, representing about 50% of the CNMI's population
item.content:encoded:
The Commonwealth Medicaid Agency reported significant gains in healthcare coverage, federal funding and operational modernization during fiscal year 2026, highlighting its role as one of the CNMI's largest healthcare safety-net programs.

According to the CMA’s report, the agency served 23,690 active Medicaid beneficiaries during the reporting period, representing about 50% of the CNMI's population based on the 2020 U.S. Census and nearly 54% of the territory's estimated 2026 population.

The report said enrollment included individuals who maintained coverage through continuity-of-coverage provisions tied to public health emergency declarations following Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi. The agency described Medicaid as a critical healthcare safety net that supports more than half of the Commonwealth's residents.

Among the year's major accomplishments was the approval of four disaster-relief state plan amendments by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The amendments support disaster-related healthcare coverage, behavioral health services and provider reimbursement. The agency also reported that federal legislation authorized an additional $21.4 million for FY 2026 Medicaid expenditures.

The report highlighted several modernization efforts, including CMS approval of the agency's FY 2026 Advance Planning Document and continued development of Medicaid information technology systems. CMA also established electronic provider enrollment portals, digitized workflow processes and upgraded office internet infrastructure from DSL to fiber service. Agency officials reported no network outages following relocation to a new facility.

Provider participation also expanded during the fiscal year. The agency approved 57 provider enrollment applications from the CNMI, Guam and the U.S. mainland, while continuing the use of letters of agreement to facilitate off-island specialty care unavailable locally. CMA processed 203 of 213 requests involving such agreements.

In its financial report, the agency reported a FY 2026 approved budget of nearly $67 million for Medical Assistance Payments and total reimbursement costs of approximately $89.7 million. On-island reimbursement expenditures totaled about $72.3 million, while off-island reimbursements amounted to roughly $17.4 million.

The agency also emphasized workforce development, reporting 18 new hires, three workforce program conversions to permanent agency positions and continued employee training initiatives. Total staffing increased from 40 to 41 employees.

Looking ahead, CMA said its priorities include implementing a new eligibility and enrollment system, expanding healthcare access through a proposed state plan amendment addressing coverage for foreign healthcare providers, pursuing a potential Section 1115 Medicaid demonstration waiver and strengthening provider compliance oversight. The agency also plans to continue exploring additional federal funding opportunities and improvements to behavioral health services.

Agency Director George J. Cruz said the agency remained focused on accountability, transparency and operational improvements while ensuring continued access to healthcare services for eligible residents throughout the Commonwealth.

item.title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
item.description: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. item.title: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
item.description: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict. On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.
item.content:encoded:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.

On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded," an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."

That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.

Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.

Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.

With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.

Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in the country's capital of Abu Dhabi this week that the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."

Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.

Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.

The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.

The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.

The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.

This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.

The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.

On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.

"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.

There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.

One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate," with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.

Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being canceled.

As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.

The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis .

Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.

"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.

item.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
item.description: Updated November 14, 2026 at 5:31 AM ChST In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 14, 2026 at 5:31 AM ChST

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare . And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests , and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene .

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."

Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling , which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.

In an earlier order in October , a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.

"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."

What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

President Trump added on Truth Social : "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.

The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."

Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."

Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

item.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
item.description: "We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world. item.content:encoded:
"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.

As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?

Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.

There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.

One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.

We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.

We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.

You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?

Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.

One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.

One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.

There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.

The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?

When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.

The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.

So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.

What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?

This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.

Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.

If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?

I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.

I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.
